about: Invented, nothing here comes from a real session. A 13 minute planning call for the copilot evals and for the copilot arm of scripts/llm_probe.py. `items` is the answer key, and the replay feeds each one back as state once it is 30 s old, as if an earlier cycle had recorded it.
lines: [00:06] them: Morning everyone, thanks for joining. The plan today is the handheld scanner rollout, then the returns backlog, and if there's time the training materials for the second shift.
[00:19] me: Sounds good. I pulled the numbers from the pilot last night, so I can start there, and Tomas can correct me where the warehouse floor saw it differently.
[00:33] them: Go ahead. How did the pilot at the Riverside site actually go, in plain terms, not the slide version?
[00:42] me: Mostly well. Picking was about eleven percent faster over the three weeks, and mispicks dropped from around two percent to under one, which is better than the vendor promised.
[00:56] them: And the battery life? That was the complaint in the first week, people were swapping units halfway through a shift and losing their place in the pick list.
[01:08] me: That one is real. The units last about six hours with the screen at full brightness, so second shift runs out before the end. Lowering brightness gets us to nearly eight.
[01:23] them: So do we just push a brightness setting, or do we need spare batteries in the charging cabinet at every site?
[01:33] me: Both, I think. The setting is free. Spare batteries are about forty dollars each and we'd want roughly one spare for every three units.
[01:47] them: Okay, let's decide that now. We buy the spares and push the brightness profile before anything goes to the Lakeside site. Nobody objects?
[01:58] me: No objection from me, that's agreed. Tomas will order the spare batteries by Thursday, he already has the purchasing login for that vendor.
[02:11] them: Yes, I can do that, Thursday works. I'll need the final unit count for Lakeside, though, otherwise I'm guessing how many to buy.
[02:22] me: Right. Priya, could you send Tomas the Lakeside unit count? She's got the latest headcount from the site manager.
[02:31] them: Priya here, yes, I'll send that today. It's a hundred and forty handhelds unless the mezzanine stays closed, in which case it drops to about a hundred and ten.
[02:46] me: When do we hear about the mezzanine?
[02:49] them: Nobody seems to know. It depends on the fire inspection, and that keeps moving. I'd plan on the higher number and we can always use the extras elsewhere.
[03:03] me: Fine by me. Now the Wi-Fi coverage at Lakeside. Riverside had two dead spots near the loading bay and the scanners would hang for ten or fifteen seconds at a time.
[03:17] them: Lakeside is a bigger building with more racking, so it'll be worse, not better. Somebody really ought to walk the floor with a signal meter before we commit to a date.
[03:29] me: Agreed, it does need doing. I don't want to volunteer anyone who isn't here, though, so let's leave it unassigned for the moment and come back to it.
[03:41] them: Okay. Then on the go-live date itself, we'd pencilled in the twelfth of next month. Is that still realistic with the battery order and the survey outstanding?
[03:54] me: The vendor quotes ten working days on batteries. If Tomas orders on Thursday we'd have them around the fifth or sixth, so yes, the twelfth is still possible, just tight.
[04:09] them: What's the fallback if it slips? Peak season starts on the twenty-fourth, and I really don't want to be changing tools during peak.
[04:19] me: If we can't go live by the seventeenth, we hold it until January. I'd rather lose a month than run a rollout through peak.
[04:30] them: I agree with that. Let's write that down as the rule: the seventeenth is the last possible date, otherwise it waits until January.
[04:41] me: Good. On to the integration with the warehouse management system. The nightly sync worked throughout the pilot, but the stock adjustments only show up the following morning.
[04:55] them: Does that actually matter to the pickers? They care whether the shelf has the item, and the morning count covers most of that.
[05:05] me: It matters for returns more than for picking. A returned item goes back on the shelf but looks unavailable until the next sync, so we sometimes tell customers it's out of stock.
[05:19] them: That's the returns backlog again, isn't it? The two problems are tangled together. Marcus has been looking at that from the customer service side.
[05:30] them: Marcus here. Yes, we've got about nine hundred returns sitting unprocessed at Riverside, and roughly a third of those are items we've marked as unavailable on the website.
[05:44] me: Nine hundred is more than I thought. How long have the oldest ones been waiting?
[05:50] them: Six weeks, the oldest. Refunds have gone out, so the customers are fine, but the stock is just sitting in cages at the back of the building.
[06:02] me: So the money's fine and the stock is the issue. What would it take to clear it?
[06:09] them: Two temp staff for two weeks would do it. That's about four thousand in agency fees. Priya has the budget for that, I think, under the seasonal line.
[06:22] them: I do, there's enough left in seasonal. Marcus, you can book the agency staff, just copy me on the purchase order so I can code it correctly.
[06:33] them: Will do, I'll book them this week so they start on Monday.
[06:39] me: Great. Longer term I'd like the returns to update stock straight away, not overnight. Is that a big change in the warehouse system?
[06:50] them: It's an API call, but the vendor charges for the module. I don't know the price offhand. We looked at it two years ago and it was silly money.
[07:02] me: Worth asking again, the volumes are different now. I could ask them, but I've got no contact there since Dana moved on.
[07:12] them: We should find out what that module costs these days. Let's not assign it right now, I'm not even sure who owns that vendor relationship any more.
[07:23] me: Okay. Parking it, but it shouldn't get lost. So, the training materials. Helen sent round a draft of the quick start card yesterday, did everyone get a chance to read it?
[07:37] them: Helen here. I'd like feedback by Wednesday if possible, because the print shop needs five working days and I want it on the floor before go-live.
[07:48] me: I read it. It's good, but it's all in English, and at least a fifth of the second shift at Lakeside would be better served in Spanish or Polish.
[07:59] them: That's a fair point. Translation isn't in my budget, though, and I don't want a bad machine translation on a safety-relevant card.
[08:10] me: Could we get one of the shift leads to review a machine translation? That would be cheaper than an agency and they'd know the terminology on the floor.
[08:20] them: That might work. Rosa on second shift speaks both Spanish and English and she's offered before. I'd want to ask her manager first, it's his call.
[08:32] me: So Helen will ask Rosa's manager whether Rosa can review the Spanish version. Polish we'll work out afterwards, I'm not aware of a Polish speaker in a lead role.
[08:44] them: Yes, I'll ask him. I can't say when, he's off until some point next week, so I'll do it when he's back.
[08:54] me: Thanks. How long does the training itself take per person? The vendor said twenty minutes, which sounded optimistic to me.
[09:03] them: At Riverside it was closer to forty minutes, including a practice pick. People who'd used smartphones picked it up quickly, and a few needed a second session.
[09:16] me: With two shifts at Lakeside and a hundred and sixty people, forty minutes each is more than a hundred hours of paid time. We'd need to stagger that.
[09:27] them: We ran groups of eight at Riverside, in the break room, one group per hour. Twenty groups would cover Lakeside, so four days if we do five sessions a day.
[09:40] me: That's workable as long as it isn't the week before go-live, when the floor will already be stretched.
[09:47] them: Agreed. We'll do training the week before that, so it finishes at least five days ahead of go-live. That's a decision as far as I'm concerned.
[09:58] me: Yes, let's take that as decided. Now, device security. IT asked whether the handhelds need a passcode, because right now they don't have one.
[10:09] them: A passcode on a shared device is a nightmare. Everyone writes it on the back in marker. What's the actual concern?
[10:17] me: The units show customer names and addresses on the pick list. If one walks out of the building, that's a reportable incident under our data policy.
[10:28] them: Hm. Can we just hide the address on the pick screen? The pickers only need the bin and the item, they've got no reason to see the address.
[10:38] me: That's a neat answer if the vendor can configure it. I don't know whether it's a setting or a change request.
[10:46] them: Tomas again. I'll check with the vendor's support line on that. Should be a quick answer, I'll have it for you by the end of next week.
[10:57] me: Perfect. Meanwhile we leave the passcode question open with IT. I'd rather not agree to anything until we know whether the address can be hidden.
[11:08] them: Fine. What about the old scanners once this is done? There's about two hundred of them, still in reasonable shape.
[11:16] me: Some might be worth keeping as spares for Riverside's cycle counts. Otherwise they have to go through the certified disposal firm because of the stored data.
[11:27] them: Let's not worry about that until after peak, it isn't urgent, and the storage cage has room.
[11:35] me: Agreed. Then one thing I'd like to raise: the weekly rollout call. Do we need it weekly until go-live, or is that overkill?
[11:44] them: I'd keep it weekly until the twelfth, then fortnightly. It's only thirty minutes, and things are moving quickly.
[11:53] me: Fine, we'll keep it weekly up to go-live. Before we wrap up, let me just read back what I have, so nobody leaves with the wrong idea.
[12:02] me: Tomas orders spare batteries by Thursday. Priya sends the Lakeside count today. Marcus books the temps this week. Helen asks Rosa's manager about the Spanish review.
[12:15] them: And feedback on the quick start card goes to Helen by Wednesday, please, everyone.
[12:21] me: Yes. And Tomas checks whether the address can be hidden on the pick screen, by the end of next week. The signal survey and the module price are still without an owner.
[12:34] them: I can take the signal survey, actually. Marcus here, I'm at Lakeside next Tuesday anyway for the returns audit, so I'll borrow the meter from IT.
[12:45] me: That's great, thanks Marcus. So the survey is yours, on Tuesday. Good meeting, everyone. Same time next week.
[12:53] them: Thanks all, talk next week.

items.text: Riverside pilot: picking about 11% faster, mispicks under 1%.
Handhelds last about 6 hours at full brightness, nearly 8 lowered.
Buy spare batteries and push the brightness profile before Lakeside.
Send Tomas the Lakeside unit count
Walk the Lakeside floor with a signal meter
Go live by the 17th at the latest, otherwise wait until January.
About 900 returns unprocessed at Riverside, a third marked unavailable online.
Book two agency temps for the returns backlog
Find out what the stock update module costs
Send Helen feedback on the quick start card
Ask Rosa's manager whether Rosa can review the Spanish card
Training finishes at least five days before go-live.
Check with vendor support whether the address can be hidden on the pick screen
Keep the rollout call weekly until go-live.
Walk the Lakeside floor with the signal meter
